questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the grievance that most directly provoked colonial resistance
questions.stem: In the heritage district plan for a colonial-era trail, you must explain which grievance provoked the sharpest colonial resistance in 1775.

options.text: Taxation without representation, since colonists were charged by a body they did not elect
The quartering of British soldiers in private houses during peacetime
options.misconception: treats troop quarters as the central grievance

options.text: The closure of western lands to settlement beyond the Appalachian ridge
options.misconception: mistakes a settlement grievance for the tax grievance

options.text: The slow delivery of post between colonies and the mother country
options.misconception: believes a postal complaint drove the revolt

questions.explanation: Colonists objected most to taxes set by a parliament in which they had no representatives, and this drove the rights petitions before fighting began. Troops and land policy were secondary issues.
questions.hint: Ask which authority imposed the disputed taxes.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how Enlightenment arguments changed eighteenth-century political debate
questions.stem: In the riverside park plan, the interpretive panel must explain how Enlightenment arguments about rights changed political debate in the 1780s.

options.text: Enlightenment writers argued that all government rested on consent, so colonial claims followed from European debate
options.misconception: assumes colonial claims arose with no local trigger

options.text: Enlightenment writers supplied a vocabulary of natural rights that colonists used to argue against inherited authority

options.misconception: reduces Enlightenment thought to toleration alone

options.text: Enlightenment ideas reached the colonies only after the wars, through academic printing presses
options.misconception: dates the spread of print ideas after the conflicts

questions.explanation: Revolutionaries borrowed the language of natural rights and consent to make old hierarchies seem illegitimate. A purely European origin, a toleration-only reading and a post-war arrival all miss how the ideas were used.
questions.hint: Focus on the language the colonists borrowed.

questions.learningObjective: Infer rural discontent from a municipal account

options.text: The town had escaped the fiscal crisis entirely, since no new levies were recorded
options.misconception: reads the account as proof of no fiscal strain

options.text: The account shows urban unrest alone, with the countryside entirely untouched
options.misconception: restricts discontent to the towns

options.text: Tax and price burdens were falling on the same rural households, sharpening local resentment
The municipal authorities had won the argument over the royal loan
options.misconception: claims the tax dispute was already settled

questions.explanation: New taxes on staple foods and a disputed loan both pressed on the same village households, which is the kind of pressure that made 1788-89 explosive. The account rules out an untouched countryside and a settled dispute.

options.text: It proved that royal authority could only be broken by a professional army
options.misconception: believes the rising required trained soldiers

options.text: It released political prisoners who had been held there for years
options.misconception: claims the fortress held mostly political captives

options.text: It seized the royal treasury and funded the new government for a decade
options.misconception: invents a captured treasury that funded a decade

options.text: It became the symbol of a population overturning royal authority

options.misconception: describes the Terror as a simple suspension of law

options.text: It claimed the Terror had already ended, so no emergency powers were still in force
options.misconception: claims the Terror was over in 1793

It insisted the Terror was a temporary measure to protect propertied citizens' interests alone
options.misconception: frames the Terror as purely a property defence

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Infer the reach of the Napoleonic Code from a legal extract

stimulus.body: An article of the 1804 civil code states that the law judges only declared acts, and that agreements lawfully made hold the force of law between the parties who made them.

questions.stem: In the courthouse renewal memo, the planner must explain what this article indicates about the new legal order.

options.text: The code limited law to written acts and made lawful agreements enforceable between the parties
The code allowed officials to judge undeclared intentions whenever they wished
options.misconception: reads the article as a licence for official judgement

options.text: The code abolished private contracts so that all exchange ran through state courts
options.misconception: misreads the article as abolishing private agreements

options.text: The code left customary law untouched and added nothing of its own
options.misconception: treats the article as proof the code was inert

questions.explanation: Restricting law to declared acts and giving force to lawful agreements is the code's hallmark: a unified, secular, written rule that bound property and contract. It did not license official judgement or abolish private bargains.
questions.hint: Note what the article says about undeclared acts.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the principle asserted in a colonial petition

options.text: That taxation required the consent of those who paid it

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how bread prices drove popular unrest in 1789
questions.stem: In the market square redesign memo, the planner must explain why the cost of bread shaped the mood of Parisian crowds in the spring of 1789.

options.text: Bread prices rose because the crown had ordered a new uniform loaf size for bakers
options.misconception: blames a regulation change for the price rise

options.text: Crowds reacted to bread prices because flour had become a form of legal tender
options.misconception: claims bread functioned as official currency

options.text: Bread was most of poor families' food, so its price directly measured their living standards
The crown had banned the sale of bread entirely during the harvest shortage
options.misconception: invents a prohibition on selling bread

questions.explanation: For most urban households bread was the bulk of the diet, so a sharp rise in its price was felt immediately as falling living standards. That is why grain shortage and bread queues sit at the centre of the early revolutionary crisis.

questions.topic: Declaration of the Rights of Man
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Declaration of Rights of Man used universal language
questions.stem: In the civic education wing memo, the curriculum note must explain why the Declaration of the Rights of Man was written in universal terms rather than as a list of French grievances.

options.text: A universal formulation asserted a standard every government could be held to, not just French complaints
A universal formulation was a legal device to prevent the document being reprinted abroad
options.misconception: invents a copyright purpose for the declaration

options.text: The assembly deliberately avoided naming any right so that no group could object
options.misconception: suggests the text named no rights at all

options.text: The universal wording was drafted by foreign jurists who knew no French conditions
options.misconception: attributes the text to outside drafter ignorance

questions.explanation: By stating rights as universal, the declaration turned a political programme into a standard that any regime, including future ones, would be measured against. That reach is the point, not a way of evading specific complaints.
questions.hint: Ask what a universal claim allows later readers to do.

questions.learningObjective: Infer the meaning of the Bastille's fall from a parish record

options.misconception: dismisses the event's wider significance

questions.learningObjective: Identify the central claim of a Haitian proclamation

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tactic described in a committee minute

stimulus.body: A committee minute from 1774 records the decision to boycott imported tea, to stop paying the tea duty, and to send the surplus tea back to the harbour rather than sell it.

questions.stem: In the quayside heritage memo, the planner must explain the tactic described in the minute.

options.text: An armed raid on the harbour to seize goods held by the crown
options.misconception: reads the minute as planning military action

options.text: Non-importation and non-payment, refusing to buy taxed goods and coercing merchants through pressure
A petition to the crown asking for the duty to be collected by the colonial assembly
options.misconception: misreads the minute as a request to the crown

options.text: An agreement among merchants to set fixed prices for tea sold in the town
options.misconception: confuses a boycott with a price agreement

questions.explanation: The minute describes economic coercion: refuse to buy taxed tea, refuse the duty, and make the movement visible at the docks. That is boycott and non-payment, not a raid, a petition or a price cartel.
questions.hint: Ask what the committee asked people not to do.

options.misconception: gives the power to parliament rather than tribunals

questions.explanation: Special tribunals turned criticism of the government into a matter for the criminal court, so opposition had to be silent. Protection of critics, a late timing and a parliamentary power all misdescribe the mechanism.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Declaration of the Rights of Man
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Declaration became a model for later constitutions
questions.stem: In the sculpture park memo, the planner must explain why the Declaration of the Rights of Man became a model for later constitutions.

options.text: It set out a detailed budget and tax schedule that later states copied unchanged
options.misconception: treats the declaration as a financial document

options.text: It was the first text to describe the physical layout of a modern capital city
options.misconception: misdirects the declaration to urban planning

options.text: It stated rights and the limits of government in a form that later constitutions could adopt
It was secretly preserved in one library and only discovered in the nineteenth century
options.misconception: invents a lost and rediscovery story

questions.explanation: Because it set out individual rights and the principle that authority derives from the nation in a portable form, later constitutions could borrow its structure. A budget, a city plan and a lost manuscript are not what made it influential.
questions.hint: Ask what later constitution writers could take from it.

questions.learningObjective: Infer local memory of occupation from an inscription

The town accepted the occupation and honoured those who served its administration
options.misconception: reads the inscription as collaboration with the occupier

options.misconception: invents the destruction of the town

options.text: The town kept no record of the wars because its inhabitants had all left
options.misconception: claims the population entirely departed

questions.explanation: Joining a rising in 1813 and later burial with honours from the restored authorities show a town that resisted and was rewarded for it. The inscription points away from collaboration, destruction or an empty village.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the change the Napoleonic Code made to property ownership
questions.stem: In the property law museum note, the planner must explain which change the Napoleonic Code made to the ownership of property.

options.text: It confirmed ownership as secure and equal for all, and ended feudal dues on land
It returned land to feudal lords who had lost it during the Revolution
options.misconception: claims the code restored feudal ownership

options.text: It placed all land in the hands of the state, which leased it to tenants
options.misconception: invents a nationalisation of all land

options.text: It gave each eldest son sole ownership of the family estate
options.misconception: misreads inheritance rules as primogeniture alone

questions.explanation: The code made property ownership secure, uniform and free of feudal dues, so buyers could hold land without old manorial claims. Restoring feudalism, nationalising everything and a simple eldest-son rule all invert its principles.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how colonial demands for representation produced a Continental Congress

options.text: Colonial assemblies had already agreed a permanent union with Britain, so congresses were routine
options.misconception: claims colonial union was already settled

options.text: British officials asked the colonies to elect representatives to sit in the British parliament
options.misconception: invites a demand that was never made in this form

options.misconception: reduces the congress to one colony's command

options.text: Separate colonial bodies began coordinating their own delegates when London refused redress

questions.explanation: Because each colony's own assembly felt its own petition unanswered, delegates from several colonies began meeting together as a congress. That is not union with Britain, a British invitation, nor one colony's order.

questions.learningObjective: Identify social tension shown in a bakery account

stimulus.body: A bakery account from the spring of 1789 lists wheat flour at a price well above the previous year's, and records that bakers in the eastern quarters were ordered to sell bread at a fixed rate.

options.text: The government had abolished bread entirely, leaving only a fixed-price shell

options.text: High flour costs and state price controls put bakers and officials at odds

questions.explanation: Rising flour prices squeezed bakers while the authorities fixed the price they must charge, creating a conflict over who bore the cost. Cheaper flour, abolition of bread and a proven absence of queues all fail.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the crowd chose the Bastille as its target
questions.stem: In the fortress interpretation plan, the planner must explain why the Bastille was chosen as a target by the crowd.

options.text: It was the headquarters of the grain merchants, who had raised bread prices
options.misconception: misidentifies the fortress as a merchants' hall

options.text: It embodied royal authority and the state's power to imprison at will
It housed the royal family's private apartments, so the crowd went there to find them
options.misconception: sends the crowd after the royal family

options.text: It was the only building in the district with gates sturdy enough to batter down
options.misconception: makes architectural weakness the motive

questions.explanation: Choosing that fortress was a deliberate statement about arbitrary authority and the state's power to imprison, which is why its name became the first emblem of the Revolution. Grain merchants, royal apartments and weak gates are not motives.
questions.hint: Ask what attacking it said about royal power.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how military emergency shaped the politics of the Terror
questions.stem: In the emergency powers exhibit memo, the planner must explain how the need for military victory shaped the politics of the Terror.

options.text: The Terror ended once victory was secured, because war and repression were separate concerns
options.misconception: separates wartime emergency from the Terror

options.text: Threats of invasion and revolt justified concentrating power and cutting the courts short
Military success let the government disband the revolutionary tribunals in 1794
options.misconception: invented a wartime disbandment of the tribunals

options.misconception: reduces the Terror to a pay dispute

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Infer the reach of Napoleonic reforms from an administrative bundle

stimulus.body: An archive bundle from a European city contains a printed copy of the civil code, a prefect's circular on the registration of transactions, and a schedule of standardised local courts, all dated within two years of each other.

questions.stem: In the municipal records archive memo, the planner must explain what the bundle indicates about the reach of Napoleon's reforms.

options.text: Reform was imposed through a uniform code and central administrative machinery, reaching beyond France
The bundle shows reforms arrived late and piecemeal, with no uniform code involved
options.misconception: claims the code was absent from the bundle

options.text: The bundle proves local courts were abolished and replaced entirely by military tribunals
options.misconception: mistakes a court schedule for abolition

options.text: The bundle is a private family archive, since the documents carry no official marks
options.misconception: ignores the official circular and schedule

questions.explanation: A printed code, a prefect's circular and a schedule of standard courts together show Napoleonic reform working as a system, exported and imposed. Late piecemeal change, abolished courts and a private archive do not match the evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what a code plus a circular plus a schedule add up to.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the wider Atlantic consequences of the Haitian Revolution
questions.stem: In the empire and colony exhibit memo, the planner must explain what the Haitian Revolution changed about the status of enslaved people across the Atlantic world.

options.text: Nothing changed, since the other colonies kept their own laws untouched by events in one island
options.misconception: denies any wider effect on other colonies

options.text: Enslaved people in other colonies gained legal freedom by decree from Saint-Domingue
options.misconception: claims Haitian decrees freed slaves elsewhere

options.text: European powers simply agreed to end slavery everywhere as a result
options.misconception: claims a general European abolition in 1804

options.text: The revolution raised the cost of holding slaves, giving many owners reason to free them

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the language of liberty rang hollow for enslaved people
questions.stem: In the testimony gallery memo, the planner must explain why the language of liberty in 1789 rang hollow for enslaved people.

options.text: Enslaved people had no legal standing, so a declaration of rights did not reach them
options.misconception: denies that the declaration could be used at all

options.text: Enslaved people rejected the declaration entirely and wanted only manumission papers
options.misconception: claims the declaration was wholly rejected

options.text: The claims of liberty and equality were made in a society that denied them to most of its members
The declaration was written in Latin, which few enslaved people could understand
options.misconception: misattributes the problem to the language used

questions.explanation: A colony where most people were held as property made universal rights a daily contradiction rather than a comfort. The other readings remove the contradiction by denying the claim, the audience or the document itself.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why abolition became urgent for the Atlantic powers

options.text: Because Haiti proved European armies could defeat colonial slaveholders if the war went on

options.misconception: claims the revolution closed the trade

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the reasoning used in a revolutionary decree

stimulus.body: A decree of the revolutionary government in the autumn of 1793 states that the survival of the republic requires the most severe measures and that suspected enemies of the state will be tried without delay.

questions.stem: In the justice courtyard design memo, the planner must identify the reasoning the decree uses.

options.text: That the law should be suspended until the war ended, leaving cases undecided
options.misconception: turns the decree into a suspension of law

options.text: That only the wealthy had a right to a fair trial, since the poor could not complain
options.misconception: invented a property-based right to trial

options.text: That the republic's survival demanded speed and severity against suspected enemies
That the enemies of the state had been pardoned and should be released quietly
options.misconception: inverts the decree into a pardon

questions.explanation: The decree argues a utilitarian case, survival first and therefore swift and severe action against suspected enemies. Suspending the law, restricting trial rights and pardoning enemies all invert what it says.
questions.hint: Ask what the decree says survival requires.

questions.topic: Declaration of the Rights of Man
questions.learningObjective: Explain what follows for society from a universal rights declaration
